name: Positivity ratio
statement: Fredrickson and Losada placed the boundary of human flourishing at a positive-to-negative affect ratio of 2.9013, a derivation American Psychologist later withdrew as invalid.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and their evidence differs, so they are kept apart here. The weak claim is that people who feel more positive emotions than negative ones do better, which nobody involved disputes. The strong claim is that flourishing begins at a precise threshold. Fredrickson and Losada wrote that a ratio at or above 2.9 marks flourishing mental health, named the boundary the Losada line, and estimated a second boundary at 11.6346 above which flourishing decays. The precision was the point. The numbers were said to hold for individuals, couples and business teams alike, and they came from a mathematical model rather than from data. Losada had earlier applied the Lorenz equations, a three-variable system Lorenz published in 1963 as a deliberately simplified model of convection in fluids, to coded speech in business meetings. The threshold is the positivity ratio corresponding to the value of the Lorenz control parameter at which chaotic behaviour sets in. That derivation was formally withdrawn in 2013. What was not withdrawn is the survey and diary study reported in the same article.

origin.who: Barbara L. Fredrickson and Marcial F. Losada
origin.note: The mathematics was not new in 2005. It came from Losada's 1999 paper in Mathematical and Computer Modelling, which applied the Lorenz equations to 60 eight-person business teams observed at the Capture Lab, and from Losada and Heaphy's 2004 paper in American Behavioral Scientist, which produced the algebraic link between the positivity ratio and the model's control parameter. The 2005 paper took both as given and added the threshold.

evidence: The article has a mathematical half and an empirical half. The mathematical half runs as follows. Losada and Heaphy had written the positivity ratio as P/N = (c − Y0 − 1)b⁻¹, where c is Losada's connectivity parameter, and Losada had set c equal to r, the control parameter of the Lorenz system. Fredrickson and Losada then cited the known value r = 24.7368, at which the Lorenz trajectory shows a chaotic attractor, and read off P/N = 2.9013. They called it the Losada line and wrote that a ratio of about 2.9 bifurcates the complex dynamics of flourishing from the limit cycle of languishing. An upper bound of 11.6346 was estimated the same way, on the reasoning that flourishing ends where chaotic behaviour ends. The empirical half is two student samples. Sample 1 was 87 first-year and second-year students at a large midwestern university, screened with a conservative test for depression that excluded about half the volunteers. Sample 2 was 101 first-year students from the same university. Flourishing was scored from a 33-item measure of positive psychological and social functioning taken from Keyes, giving 36 flourishers in Sample 1 and 9 in Sample 2. Each evening for 28 days participants rated 20 emotions from 0 to 4. Positive emotions counted if rated 2 or above, negative emotions if rated 1 or above, and the month's totals were divided. Mean ratios were 3.2 for flourishers against 2.3 for the rest, t(85) = 2.32, p = .01 one-tailed, ω² = .05; and 3.4 against 2.1, t(99) = 1.62, p = .05 one-tailed, ω² = .02. The authors treated it as the critical result that the two means in each sample flanked 2.9.

replication.headline: The 2.9013 threshold was demolished by mathematical argument rather than by a failed repetition, and American Psychologist withdrew the derivation while leaving the two student samples standing.
replication.detail: None of the four state values fits this case cleanly. Nobody reran the experiment. Brown, Sokal and Friedman read the mathematics instead. Their 2013 article in American Psychologist argues that the Lorenz equations were never shown to apply to human emotion, and they set out five conditions any use of differential equations must meet and find that Losada's work meets at most part of one. Their specific charges are worth separating. Losada gave no account of how continuous, deterministic, smoothly varying functions were built from coded speech acts. He set the Lorenz parameters σ = 10 and b = 8/3 by following the choice Saltzman made for illustrative convenience in 1962, and set r equal to the raw count of significant cross-correlations in an eight-person team, which makes a universal control parameter depend on team size. On the fit between model and data, which is the heart of the matter, Losada asserted that his simulated time series matched the general characteristics of the lab time series, and Brown, Sokal and Friedman note that no such empirical time series appear anywhere in his paper, that the phrase is never defined, and that the claim must therefore be taken on faith. Fredrickson and Losada described a statistical matching of model to data at p < .01, and Brown and colleagues report that no such matching is alluded to in either of the two earlier papers. Their sharpest point is that the threshold is arbitrary. Since 2.9013 follows from σ, b and an offset i by simple algebra, changing σ from 10 to 16 moves the answer to 4.1655405. The upper bound rests on a further error, because chaos in the Lorenz system does not stop above r ≈ 48, and instead alternates with narrow windows of periodicity to at least r ≈ 200. Losada declined to defend the model. Fredrickson replied in the same issue, wrote that she had neither the expertise nor the insight to defend Losada's mathematical work, and said she had come to question the framework. The correction notice, published as a one-page item in the same issue, is precise about scope. It withdraws the modelling element as invalid and with it the model-based predictions about the particular positivity ratios of 2.9 and 11.6, and states that other elements remain valid, naming the supporting literature, the data from two independent samples, and the finding that positivity ratios were higher for flourishers. So the modelling was retracted and the empirical half was not. Brown, Sokal and Friedman returned in 2014 to the empirical half, which their first paper had left alone. Reverse-engineering the published summary statistics under an equal-variance assumption, they estimate a standard deviation of about 1.78 in Sample 1 and about 2.30 in Sample 2, and conclude that roughly 36% of the nonflourishers must have had ratios above 2.9013, which is the opposite of what a threshold predicts. They also note that t(99) = 1.62 gives p = 0.0542 one-tailed, and that dichotomising participants into flourishing and nonflourishing discards the information that could show any nonlinearity at all. Their verdict is that there is no evidence for any tipping point and only weak evidence for nonlinearity of any kind.

study.cite: Brown, N. J. L., Sokal, A. D., & Friedman, H. L. (2013). The complex dynamics of wishful thinking: The critical positivity ratio. American Psychologist, 68(9), 801-813.

limits: The verdict covers 2.9013 and 11.6346 and nothing wider. Brown, Sokal and Friedman say in their own words that they do not question the idea that a higher positivity ratio is ordinarily more desirable than a lower one, and that the 3.2 against 2.3 result is unsurprising. Work on affect ratios without the magic number exists and should be kept apart from the 2005 claim. Diehl, Hay and Berg ran a 30-day diary study with 239 adults, 81 young, 81 middle-aged and 77 older, and report that higher ratios went with better mental health and that ratios rose with age. On the threshold itself their finding splits: 2.9 worked as a critical value in young adulthood and did not discriminate mental health status as well in middle-aged and older adults. Shrira and colleagues studied 123 gastric cancer patients and 84 hospital staff exposed to missile attacks, found a curvilinear relation in both, and report that the fall in maladaptive functioning levelled out at a ratio of around three and then stayed flat or rose mildly. Fredrickson cites Rego and colleagues on 595 Portuguese retail employees, with an inverted-U peaking at 3.6 to 1, and that study is named here from her description of it rather than read. Brown, Sokal and Friedman reanalysed the Rego data and argue that most of the curvature disappears once the independent variable is changed from P/N to the bounded quantity P/(P+N), which carries the same information. Their broader objection is that a regression curve estimated in one population gives no reason to expect the same curve elsewhere. Two papers on the empirical side were not read for this entry. Nickerson's 2018 comment in the Journal of Humanistic Psychology, whose title is that there is no empirical evidence for critical positivity ratios, is paywalled at Sage and behind a bot check; its abstract was read at Crossref and says she examines the mismatch between theory and the data used to test it, the methodological and statistical problems of the 2005 study, and the other studies Fredrickson cited. Shrira, Bodner and Palgi's 2016 paper in the Journal of Positive Psychology is also paywalled, and Unpaywall lists no open copy, so it is reported here only through Friedman and Brown's description, which is that the observed ratio shifts with participants' age and with the measurement approach used.
misreadings: The commonest error is to file this with the failed replications. It does not belong there. No one repeated the study and came up empty. Brown, Sokal and Friedman opened the mathematics and found that the Lorenz equations had been applied to coded speech with no justification, that the fit between model and data was asserted rather than shown, and that the threshold depends on constants a geophysicist picked for convenience in 1962. That is a different kind of failure and a more final one, because arithmetic can be checked. The second error is to say the paper was retracted. It was not, and the notice says what it covers: the modelling and the predicted ratios of 2.9 and 11.6 are withdrawn as invalid, and the two samples and their result are left standing. The third error runs the other way, treating the surviving empirical half as vindication of a ratio. It shows an association between higher ratios and flourishing in two small student samples, and Brown and colleagues argue in 2014 that the same summary statistics imply many nonflourishers sat above the line. The fourth is to attribute the critique to a journal or to positive psychology's critics generally. It is the work of Nicholas J. L. Brown, Alan D. Sokal and Harris L. Friedman, and Brown was a part-time master's student when he began it. The fifth concerns Losada's own papers. His 1999 article and the 2004 article with Emily Heaphy carry no retraction, correction or expression of concern in Crossref's record as of the date this entry was checked, and both remain citable despite being the source of the model the 2005 correction withdrew. The sixth is rounding. Dropping 2.9013 to a friendly 3 to 1 does not rescue the claim, because the objection was never to the decimal places but to the derivation that produced them.
